items.new: "You said up there, didn't you? And now look for yourself and see where your tongs are pointing. But perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber's hole (the opening in the main-top platform that timid climbers use), cook; but no, no, cook, you don't get there unless you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It's a ticklish business, but it must be done, or else it's no go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook, and hear my orders. Do you hear? Hold your hat in one hand, and clap the other on top of your heart when I'm giving my orders, cook. What! That your heart, there? — that's your gizzard! Aloft! Aloft! — that's it — now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention."
items.reason: "lubber's hole" is an unexplained nautical term, and Stubb's joke (the lazy route vs. "the regular way, round by the rigging") depends on knowing it. Brief gloss added once.

items.new: The fact is that, among his hunters at least, the whale would be considered a noble dish by all hands, were there not so much of him; but when you come to sit down before a meat-pie nearly one hundred feet long, it takes away your appetite. Only the most unprejudiced of men, like Stubb, eat cooked whale nowadays; but the Eskimos are not so fastidious. We all know how they live on whales, and keep rare old vintages of prime old train oil. Zogranda, one of their most famous doctors, recommends strips of blubber for infants, as being exceedingly juicy and nourishing. And this reminds me of certain Englishmen who long ago were accidentally left behind in Greenland by a whaling vessel: these men actually lived for several months on the moldy scraps of whales that had been left ashore after the blubber was tried out (boiled down for oil). Among the Dutch whalemen these scraps are called "fritters," which, indeed, they greatly resemble, being brown and crisp, and smelling something like old Amsterdam housewives' doughnuts, or oly-cooks, when fresh. They look so edible that the most self-denying stranger can hardly keep his hands off them.
items.reason: Resumptive "reminds me that certain Englishmen, who ... — that these men actually lived" is an 1851 construction that trips read-aloud. Restructured with a colon; all content kept.

items.new: But sometimes, especially on the Line (the Equator) in the Pacific, this plan will not answer at all, because such incalculable hosts of sharks gather around the moored carcass that if it were left so for, say, six hours at a stretch, little more than the skeleton would be visible by morning. In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish are not so abundant, their wondrous voracity can at times be considerably reduced by vigorously stirring them up with sharp whaling-spades — a procedure which, nevertheless, in some instances only seems to tickle them into still greater activity. But it was not so in the present case with the Pequod's sharks; though, to be sure, any man unused to such sights who had looked over her side that night would almost have thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it.
items.reason: "on the Line" (sailors' term for the Equator) is not explained anywhere nearby and stops a first-time reader. Brief gloss.
